topics.title: Comments are ignored by the compiler
topics.body: `//` comments out the rest of the line and `/* ... */` spans lines. Comments document intent; they never change the program, and the compiler discards them before linking.

topics.title: The standard you compiled with
topics.body: `__cplusplus` is a predefined macro that reports the language standard as a number: `201703` means C++17. It is useful when a build must prove which standard produced it.

interview.q: Why is C++ compiled instead of interpreted, and what does that buy the program?
interview.answer: The compiler translates the whole translation unit to machine code ahead of time, so type errors surface before the program runs and execution needs no interpreter in the loop. That is why a C++ binary starts fast and has predictable performance.

It asks the preprocessor to copy the contents of the iostream header into the translation unit, which declares `std::cout`, `std::cin` and the stream operators. It does not link anything by itself; the linker brings in the standard library implementation.

mcq.q: What does `return 0;` at the end of `main` report?
options: Successful termination to the operating system
mcq.answer: Successful termination to the operating system
mcq.why: The return value of `main` is the process exit status; zero means success.

mcq.q: Which g++ command builds `main.cpp` into an executable named `app`?
mcq.why: The source file is compiled and linked, and `-o app` names the output binary.

topics.title: Escape sequences you will actually use
topics.body: `\t` inserts a tab, `\n` ends the line, `\\` prints a backslash and `\"` prints a quote. Each sequence is one character in the string even though it is typed as two.

topics.title: Reading fields from a string stream
topics.body: `std::istringstream` behaves like `std::cin` but reads from a string, which makes parsing testable without waiting for a keyboard. `>>` splits on whitespace and converts to the requested type.

interview.q: Why does `std::cin >> name` stop at the first space?
interview.answer: The extraction operator treats whitespace as the field separator, so it reads one token. A full line needs `std::getline`, and mixing the two requires clearing the leftover newline first.

interview.q: Why does `std::setw` affect only the next output field?
interview.answer: Width is consumed by the single insertion that follows it, while flags such as `std::left`, `std::fixed` and the fill character persist. That is why an aligned table repeats `setw` per column but sets the alignment once.

options: The padding side for the next output field
mcq.answer: The padding side for the next output field
mcq.why: It makes subsequent width-padded output align to the left until changed.

topics.title: auto deduces a type, it does not guess
topics.body: `auto` takes the type from the initializer, so `auto count = 7` is an `int` and `auto ratio = 7.0` is a `double`. An uninitialized `auto` is a compile error because there is nothing to deduce from.

topics.title: constexpr is computed at compile time
topics.body: A `constexpr` function can run during compilation when its arguments are constants, and `static_assert` then verifies the result before the program ever executes.

tasks.title: Report four type sizes
tasks.statement: Print the sizes of `char`, `int`, `long long` and `bool`, separated by single spaces.

interview.q: When should a value be `const` instead of `constexpr`?
interview.answer: `const` promises the value will not change after initialization but may be computed at runtime; `constexpr` requires it to be computable at compile time. Use `constexpr` when the value must participate in compile-time checks or array bounds.

interview.q: Why does `unsigned` subtraction wrap instead of going negative?
interview.answer: Unsigned arithmetic is defined modulo two to the power of the type width, so subtracting past zero wraps to a huge positive value. That is well-defined, not undefined, and it is exactly why counts that can go negative should be signed.

mcq.q: What is the type of `auto x = 5 / 2.0;`?
mcq.why: The literal `2.0` is a double, so the division and the deduced type are double.

mcq.q: What must a `constexpr` variable be initialized with?
mcq.why: Its value has to be known during compilation, which is what makes it usable in compile-time contexts.

topics.title: Integer division and modulus together
topics.body: `/` between two ints truncates toward zero and `%` returns the remainder with the sign of the left operand. The two results always satisfy `a == (a / b) * b + a % b`.

topics.title: Prefix and postfix increment differ
topics.body: `a++` yields the old value and then increments, while `++a` increments and yields the new value. Reading both in one expression is where beginners lose track of the order.

interview.q: What is operator precedence and why does it matter?
interview.answer: Precedence decides which operator binds first when several appear without parentheses; `*` before `+`, for example. When the intent is not obvious, parentheses are cheaper than a reader re-deriving the table.

interview.q: Why is `static_cast<double>(a) / b` safer than relying on implicit conversion?
interview.answer: It states the conversion at the exact point it matters, so the division is floating point even if both operands are ints. Implicit conversion can happen later than the author expects, leaving integer division in place.

mcq.why: Five goes into seventeen three times with a remainder of two.

mcq.q: Which expression increments `a` and yields the new value?
mcq.why: The prefix form updates first and yields the updated value.

topics.title: switch falls through without break
topics.body: Cases share code by stacking labels, and execution continues into the next case until a `break` or the end of the switch. That is a feature when intentional and a bug when forgotten.

topics.title: Guard clauses flatten a decision tree
topics.body: Returning early for each rejected case keeps the happy path at one indentation level. The alternative is a pyramid of nested `if`s where the reader must remember every condition to reach the end.

interview.q: Which types can be used in a `switch` condition?
interview.answer: Integral types and enums, plus `char`. Floating-point values and strings cannot be switched on because the case labels must be compile-time integral constants.

interview.q: When is a chain of `else if` better than `switch`?
interview.answer: When the conditions are ranges or unrelated predicates, because `switch` only matches exact constants. A `switch` over an enum is still clearer when every enumerator is handled.

mcq.q: What happens when a `switch` case has no `break`?
options: Execution continues into the next case
mcq.answer: Execution continues into the next case
mcq.why: Fallthrough is the specified behaviour, which is why a missing break changes the result.
The remainder operator returns zero when the division is exact.

topics.title: do-while runs once before checking
topics.body: The body of a `do-while` executes before the condition is tested, so it always runs at least once. That makes it the right shape for "ask once, then repeat while the answer is invalid".

topics.title: Range-based for reads every element
topics.body: `for (int m : marks)` visits each element in order and copies it into `m`; `for (const int& m : marks)` avoids the copy. The loop cannot run past the container because it uses its iterators.

interview.answer: `for` when the iteration count or the counter is the point of the loop, `while` when the loop ends on a condition that is not a counter, such as reading until end of input.

interview.q: Why does a range-based for not need an index?
interview.answer: It iterates with `begin()` and `end()`, so the container supplies the bounds. That removes the off-by-one class of bug and works for containers that have no index at all.

mcq.q: How many times does a `do-while` body run when the condition is false from the start?
mcq.why: The body runs before the first condition test.

mcq.q: Which loop is guaranteed to visit every element of a vector in order?
mcq.why: The range form uses the container bounds exactly once, without an index to get wrong.

topics.title: Default arguments fill the gap
topics.body: A default argument is used only when the caller omits that argument; it is written once in the declaration. Defaults must be trailing, so a parameter with a default cannot precede one without.

topics.title: Passing by reference changes the caller
topics.body: A reference parameter is another name for the caller’s object, so writing through it mutates the original. Passing by value would modify only the copy and leave the caller unchanged.

interview.q: What is function overloading resolved by?
interview.answer: The compiler matches the call against each declaration’s parameter list and return type is not part of the signature, so two functions cannot differ only by return type. Ambiguous conversions make the call a compile error.

interview.q: Why prefer `const T&` for a read-only parameter?
interview.answer: It avoids copying a large object while still promising the callee cannot modify it, and it binds to temporaries. For small scalars a plain value is usually cheaper than a reference.

mcq.q: Which call is ambiguous for `void f(int); void f(double);`?
mcq.why: A float converts equally well to int and double, so neither overload is a better match.

mcq.q: What does a default argument allow?
mcq.why: The omitted argument is filled with the declared default at the call site.

topics.title: split a string with find and substr
topics.body: `find` returns the position of a character or `std::string::npos`, and `substr(pos, len)` copies a slice. Combining them splits a record without a regular expression.

topics.title: string_view is a non-owning window
topics.body: `std::string_view` stores a pointer and a length, so taking a substring or passing it to a function copies no characters. It is valid only while the underlying string is alive.

interview.answer: It is the value returned by `find` when nothing matched, defined as the largest representable size type. Comparing against it is the check, not comparing against `-1` by hand.
When it outlives the string it points into, or when that string reallocates. It owns nothing, so a dangling view reads freed memory with no warning.

mcq.q: What does `mail.substr(0, at)` return when `at` is the position of `@`?
mcq.why: `substr` starts at 0 and copies `at` characters, which stops before the @.

mcq.q: Which type stores a pointer and a length without owning characters?
mcq.why: A view is a non-owning window over existing characters.
